title: French Africa
capsule: French Africa was the collective designation for France's colonial holdings on the African continent, which expanded dramatically during the Scramble for Africa (1880s–1900s) to encompass the vast interior of West and Equatorial Africa, as well as Madagascar, Tunisia, Morocco, and Algeria — together covering roughly 11 million square kilometers by 1914, the second largest African colonial empire after Britain's. French West Africa (established 1895) and French Equatorial Africa (1910) were federated groupings administered from Dakar and Brazzaville respectively, providing cheap raw materials and soldiers (the tirailleurs sénégalais) for France. The twin shocks of World War II — France's defeat and the Atlantic Charter — energized African nationalist movements; the 1956 loi-cadre devolved some powers, and in 1960 almost all French sub-Saharan territories became independent, while Algeria won independence after a brutal war in 1962.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Formal colonial boundaries are documented by the Berlin Conference (1884–85) agreements, bilateral treaties, and colonial administrative maps; the outer extents of Saharan and Sahel territories are well surveyed from the early 20th century; high confidence for post-1900 extents, moderate for pre-1885 frontiers.
